source.title_on_document: How LLMs Distort Our Written Language

supplement.where: Same PDF: contents p. 21, appendices A-I on pp. 22-95. Contents-page section labels are outdated; locators follow body headings.
supplement.holds: User-study instructions, questionnaires and demographics (pp. 22-26); editing prompts and semantic, lexical, POS and emotion robustness figures (pp. 26-43); classifier prompts (pp. 44-46); Table 1 with peer-review category percentages, z statistics and p-values (p. 46); essay examples and transcripts (pp. 47-95). No scalar across-writer diversity effect or corresponding numerical uncertainty is supplied for S1 or S2. Numerical average within-essay semantic shifts are printed in figure images, including Figure 1; these are not diversity effects.

paper_design_summary: An online experiment reports 100 Prolific participants randomized to write an argumentative essay with or without gpt-4o-mini; analyses compare controls with observed low- and extensive-use subgroups, and Figure 4b contains 99 directly counted essay observations while the overall analyzed participant count remains unresolved (pp. 4-5, 8-13). A second study analyzes automated revisions of archived essays from 86 students against their human revisions after expert feedback, while a third analyzes scientific criteria and scores in 18k naturally occurring ICLR reviews classified as human- or LLM-written (pp. 5-7, 13-14). An eight-person preliminary protocol pilot informed the use classification; pilot/main participant overlap is not stated, and no pilot creativity/diversity outcome is reported (p. 5).

studies.label: Human user study: argumentative essay writing

assignment.what_was_assigned: People were randomized to no LLM access or unrestricted access to an embedded gpt-4o-mini during writing. The reported LLM and LLM-Influenced groups were not randomized arms: the classification rule was decided before analysis, informed by a protocol pilot, and applied to self-reports and transcripts. LLM-Influenced required self-reported generation of less than 40% of the text, corroborated against transcripts (pp. 4-5, Section 3.1).
assignment.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions:
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1, Human Study; p. 5, usage-group classification

arms.name: Control / Human User (no LLM)
arms.description: Randomized no-LLM control; no AI assistant or internet permitted during essay writing. The 45 people are reported at assignment, not as an outcome-specific analyzed denominator (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 22, Appendix A.4).

arms.name: AI-assisted condition (gpt-4o-mini available)
arms.description: Randomized access to embedded gpt-4o-mini, with 55 people reported at assignment. The subsequent use classification identified 28 out of 55 as LLM-Influenced and 12 out of 55 as refusing to use the LLM to generate the essay. These overlapping descriptions are not additional randomized arms or documented complete-case counts; the extensive-use subgroup count is not explicitly printed (pp. 4-5, Section 3.1).

participants.exclusions: The methods report 100 people and randomized allocation of 45 controls and 55 AI-access participants (p. 4), with 28 of 55 classified as LLM-Influenced (p. 5). Figure 4b contains 99 essay observations: 43 Human-User circles, 29 LLM-Influenced triangles and 27 LLM crosses, directly counted from the PDF vector graphics, excluding legend symbols (p. 8). These plotted group counts conflict with the methods; the figure's two AI-use groups sum to 56, not the reported 55. Figure 6 percentages are compatible with the plotted group counts but do not independently establish analyzed denominators (p. 10). The overall and arm-level analyzed participant counts therefore remain null. No exclusion, attrition or participant-flow explanation is supplied; the discrepancy cannot be converted into an exclusion count. Figure 12 attributes incomplete demographic totals to item nonresponse (p. 26). Pilot participants are not added to S1, and pilot/main overlap is unknown. No intention-to-treat analysis is claimed. Figure-count provenance: PyMuPDF doc[7].get_xobjects() identifies Form XObject 1429; its decoded stream has 43 /M0 Do, 29 /M1 Do and 27 /M2 Do invocations. Objects 1781, 1782 and 1783 are circle, triangle and cross markers; the legend shapes are drawn separately.
participants.who: Native-English-speaking Prolific participants residing in the United States. The paper reports 100 randomized participants; the overall analyzed count is unresolved. Figure 12 acknowledges demographic item nonresponse.
participants.quote: We conducted a human user study of 100 participants
participants.locator: pp. 4-5, Section 3.1; p. 8, Figure 4b (direct marker count); p. 10, Figure 6; p. 22, Appendix A.1 and A.3-A.4; p. 26, Figure 12

ai_tool.how_used: Participants could use the embedded LLM however they chose while writing; conversations and final essays were recorded. Other LLMs and internet sources were prohibited. Use intensity was classified from actual use (pp. 4-5; p. 22, Appendix A.3). gpt-4o was a separate outcome-classification judge (p. 7).

task.description: Argumentative essay answering Does money lead to happiness? In scope through cross-writer semantic comparisons; there is no independent creativity rating of the essay (p. 4; p. 8, Figure 4).
task.duration: Whole-study estimate 35 minutes, maximum 1 hour; essay-only duration not stated (p. 22, Appendix A.1).

outcomes.name: Semantic diversity / clustering of final essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each final essay is embedded with MiniLM-L6-v2 and projected using t-SNE. Group spread/clustering is interpreted as diversity/homogenization. No scalar pairwise-similarity, centroid-distance or dispersion effect is reported. Actual-use subgroups split the randomized AI-access arm; no combined AI-access-versus-control estimate is printed (pp. 8-9). n_units = 99 is a direct count of Figure 4b's plotted observations, not a printed N: 43 Human-User circles + 29 LLM-Influenced triangles + 27 LLM crosses, excluding legend symbols (p. 8). These counts apply only to this figure and do not settle overall analyzed participant or other-outcome denominators; they conflict with the methods' allocation/classification counts (pp. 4-5).

contrasts.reported: Extensive-use essays form a distinct small cluster, whereas control essays occupy a broader region. No numerical diversity effect, SD, SE, CI, test, or plotted analysis N is printed. This selects an actual-use subgroup from the randomized AI-access arm.
contrasts.locator: pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and Section 4.2

contrasts.reported: LLM-Influenced essays are described as occupying a similar distribution to control essays. Visual comparison only; no numerical difference or equivalence test reported.
contrasts.locator: pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and Section 4.2

diversity_detail.metric: Qualitative dispersion/clustering in two-dimensional t-SNE; no scalar diversity index.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Final essays from different writers, jointly displayed and labeled Human User, LLM-Influenced or LLM; no all-pairs or centroid calculation reported.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No diversity SE, CI, bootstrap, permutation or other inferential uncertainty reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Lower denotes less diversity, not a direction along an embedding axis. AI was available to both use-defined AI subgroups during writing; random assignment was to access, not use intensity. The task asks each participant for one final essay (p. 4; p. 22, Appendix A.3-A.4), and Figure 4b is captioned as each essay produced in the RCT. The directly counted 99 essay observations therefore support more than 50 analyzed writers for this outcome, without establishing an exact overall analyzed N. See participants.exclusions for reproducible PDF marker-count provenance.

studies.label: ArgRewrite-v2: automated LLM revisions versus original human revisions

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was assigned AI help. Researchers supplied archived initial drafts and expert feedback to three LLMs and compared automated revisions with existing human revisions. Editing/feedback variants manipulate models on the same source essays, not people. Within refers to repeated versions of source documents (pp. 5-6).
assignment.quote: we then construct a dataset of LLM-generated D2 drafts.

arms.name: Human D1 (original draft reference)
arms.description: Original unassisted essays from the same source students; reference locations for revision arrows, not a separate sample (pp. 5-7, sections 3.1-3.2).

arms.name: Human-revised D2 (ArgRewrite-v2)
arms.description: The same 86 source students revised their own D1 essays in response to expert human feedback; no AI was available. Code other_aid records this feedback. Human D1 and D2 are repeated versions from the same people and must not be added as independent samples (pp. 5-7, Section 3.1 and Section 3.2).

arms.name: gpt-5-mini revisions
arms.description: Automated revisions across general, minimal, grammar, completion and expansion instructions, with/without expert feedback. No people in this model condition (p. 6; pp. 26-43).

arms.name: gemini-2.5-flash revisions
arms.description: Same source drafts and editing/feedback variants; no people assigned to the model (p. 6; pp. 26-43).

arms.name: claude-haiku revisions
arms.description: Same drafts/variants. Plots label Claude 3.5 Haiku, whereas Appendix I examples label Claude Haiku 4.5; model version is inconsistent (p. 6; pp. 9, 34-37, 61, 81-82).

participants.exclusions: No corpus exclusions stated. The paper identifies 86 university students (p. 5) and analyzes 86 essays (p. 7). These are reused people; model revisions are not new participants.
participants.who: University students in ArgRewrite-v2; essays collected in 2021 and corpus released in 2022 before widespread LLM writing assistance.
participants.quote: ArgRewrite-v2 (Kashefi et al., 2022) is a dataset of argumentative writing revisions collected from 86 university students.
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 7, Section 3.2, PCA of Embedding Representations

ai_tool.name_model: gpt-5-mini; gemini-2.5-flash; claude-haiku (Claude 3.5 Haiku in plots; Claude Haiku 4.5 in Appendix I examples)
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated revisions of archived drafts under general, minimal, grammar, completion and expansion modes, with/without existing expert feedback. The actual minimal-edit prompt asks to rewrite the essay and keep a similar word count; the grammar prompt asks to revise for grammar; completion uses the first paragraph and expansion requests more detail and depth. No source participant received the generated revisions as AI assistance (p. 6, Section 3.1; p. 26, Appendix B.1).

task.description: Argumentative op-eds for or against self-driving cars. Human D2 followed expert feedback; models subsequently generated D2 from the same D1 inputs. AI-versus-human output, not after_ai (pp. 5-6).

outcomes.name: Semantic convergence across revised essays
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: PCA visualizations pair original and revised embeddings and show revision directions. The paper interprets common-direction shifts across writers as homogenization. Robustness variants use MiniLM-L6-v2/gemini-004, different model editors, edit modes and feedback conditions (p. 1, Figure 1; p. 9, Figure 5; pp. 26-34, Figures 13-25). Numeric within-essay shift labels are separate in S2-O2: they are not between-writer diversity effects. The 86 units are paired original D1 and revised D2 drafts per revision condition, based on the 86 source essays; each pair is linked by a semantic-change arrow (p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 9, Figure 5 caption).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Automated revisions by the three LLMs
contrasts.reported: Human revisions show smaller, more varied directional changes; model revisions shift essays in a common direction toward a different semantic region. No scalar between-writer diversity difference or uncertainty is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 1, Figure 1; p. 9, Figure 5 and Section 4.2; pp. 26-34, Appendix B.2-B.4, Figures 13-25

diversity_detail.metric: Qualitative convergence/common direction of D1-to-D2 arrows in PCA; no aggregate pairwise similarity or dispersion effect.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: MiniLM-L6-v2 in Figure 1 (p. 1) and the Appendix B.3 heading (p. 29); gemini-004 in Figure 5 (p. 9) and Appendix B.2 (p. 26). Figures 18-22 captions instead print MiniLM-L6-004 (pp. 29-31); the exact appendix checkpoint cannot be settled from these inconsistent labels.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Embeddings from different students, pairing D1 and D2 within each source essay and inspecting common displacement across essays; not all between-writer pairs.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No inferential uncertainty for between-writer diversity reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Context only: automated revisions of historical drafts, with no human receiving AI help. Mixed availability refers to human and model output sources. Direction follows the authors' homogenization interpretation; large within-essay shift alone does not establish reduced between-writer dispersion. Figure 5 has a feedback-label conflict: its plot title says With Feedback, while its caption says without access to expert feedback (p. 9). This record does not select a feedback condition from that figure.

outcomes.name: Lexical change from the original draft (Jensen-Shannon divergence)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: JSD between D1 and D2 unigram distributions over a global vocabulary, evaluated per source essay. Higher means more vocabulary replacement in the same essay, not inter-person lexical diversity. Appendix B.5 varies five editing modes, expert feedback and all three models (pp. 35-37, Figures 26-30).

contrasts.treatment_arm: claude-haiku: general revision with expert feedback
contrasts.reported: Figure 7 reports Mean Distance 0.476 for Claude 3.5 Haiku / claude-haiku. Section 4.4 describes the human distribution as centered around 0.2-0.3 JSD; this is not a human mean or SD. It describes gpt-5-mini divergence as nearly triple the human baseline, with many essays above 0.7. No effect or precision is derived.

outcomes.name: Grammatical revision profile: part-of-speech changes
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Relative POS frequency changes from original human D1, for human D2 and model revisions. Plotted categories: adjectives, adpositions, adverbs, auxiliaries, coordinating conjunctions, determiners, nouns, pronouns and verbs. All edit modes/feedback/models are variants (p. 11, Figure 8 right; pp. 38-42, Figures 31-35). These are linguistic categories, not creative-idea categories.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Automated revisions by the three LLMs
contrasts.reported: Section 4.5 reports human changes typically under 5% per POS category; LLM changes relative to D1: adjectives increase 57-90%, coordinating conjunctions increase 13-90%, pronouns decrease 40-60%, and determiners decrease 25-50%. For minimal edits, adjectives increase 40-87% and pronouns decrease 31-56%. These are prose-reported ranges, not calculated AI-minus-human effects or reconstructed mode-specific values. The same paragraph also reports, for gpt-5-mini, an 88% increase in coordinating conjunctions, a 27% increase in nouns, and a 61% decrease in pronouns; the precise edit mode for this sentence is not explicitly identified.

assignment.what_was_assigned: No aid was assigned. Existing reviews were classified with Pangram AI and papers with one human-written and one entirely LLM-generated review selected. Observational corpus analysis matched by reviewed paper, not an experiment with reviewers (p. 6).
assignment.quote: We selected only those papers with one review written entirely by a human and one written entirely by an LLM

arms.name: Reviews classified as entirely human-written
arms.description: 9k reviews; not a distinct reviewer count (p. 13, Figure 11).

arms.name: Reviews classified as entirely LLM-generated
arms.description: 9k reviews detected with Pangram; underlying writing models and actual reviewer use unobserved (pp. 6, 13).

participants.exclusions: Only papers with both an entirely human-written and an entirely LLM-generated review selected. Distinct reviewers not counted; the full conference review count is not the analysis sample or a people count (p. 6).

eligibility.reason: S1 randomized access to AI, but its reported diversity comparisons select extensive-use and low-use subgroups after assignment. These are observational comparisons of actual use, not comparisons of the randomized access arms (PDF pp. 4-5, 8-9, Figure 4b and Section 4.2). Self-reported creativity does not qualify (PDF p. 24, Appendix A.6). S2 compares automated revisions of archived drafts with human revisions and supplies AI-versus-human context (PDF pp. 5-6). No reported comparison establishes an eligible randomized creativity or diversity effect.

one_line_finding: In the study reporting 100 randomized participants, heavy LLM users' essays clustered semantically, with self-rated creativity 3.41 versus 3.95 and neutral stances 66.7% versus 39.5% in controls; use intensity was not randomized and the overall analyzed N is unresolved (pp. 4-5, 8, 10; Figures 4 and 6).
open_questions: What reconciles S1's reported 100 randomized participants, allocation 45/55 and 28 LLM-Influenced users with Figure 4b's directly counted 43/29/27 essay observations (99 total)? Exact overall and arm analyzed counts remain null; exclusions, participant flow and other-outcome denominators are not supplied. The figure count is documented in S1-O1, not substituted for all outcomes. Figure 6 percentages are compatible with these marker counts but are not independent evidence of denominators; several tests print t(69) (pp. 4-5, 8, 10, 13).

A numerical diversity effect with participant-appropriate uncertainty for the full randomized AI-access-versus-control comparison is absent. S1 Figure 4b displays observed-use groups, and S2 displays revision arrows; neither supplies a scalar between-writer diversity effect or its uncertainty (pp. 1, 8-9, 26-34).

The generation model is called claude-haiku in methods, Claude-3.5-Haiku in Figure 25, and Claude Haiku 4.5 in Appendix I. The PDF cannot establish a single exact version across all analyses/examples (p. 6; p. 34; p. 61).

The Appendix B.3 heading says MiniLM-L6-v2, but Figures 18-22 captions say MiniLM-L6-004. The exact checkpoint for those appendix plots needs clarification; Figure 1 explicitly identifies MiniLM-L6-v2 (p. 1; pp. 29-31).

Figure 5 title says With Feedback, but its caption says without access to expert feedback. A corrected label or underlying data is needed before selecting a feedback-specific numerical result from that figure (p. 9).

The clarity-as-strength test is z = 11.00, p < 0.001 in Figure 11, z = 14.37, p < 0.00001 in Section 4.8, and z = 14.3704 with printed p = 0.0000 in Table 1. Figure 11 gives a human baseline of 17%; Table 1 gives G1 5.76 and G2 3.89 with a denominator of three times the review count. Preserve these distinct presentations; the PDF does not settle the intended test or explicitly define the Table 1 G1/G2 source mapping (pp. 13-14, 46).
ICLR recommendation-score claims differ: abstract full point higher; Section 4.8 means 4.43 and 4.13, described there as 10% higher. The PDF does not resolve these descriptions (pp. 1, 14).

Did any of the eight pilot participants also enter the main study, or was repeat participation prohibited? The source identifies a preliminary phase but does not establish participant nonoverlap (p. 5, Section 3.1; pp. 22-26, Appendix A).
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 after reading the entire markdown conversion, including all appendices and examples through p. 95, and checking source passages for all three challenge problems. The assignment challenge lists no problems. All three listed outcome/people problems were corrected. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the earlier review record; final.challenge_resolution records the subsequent corrections. Eligibility facts and recorded numerical results were checked against PDF text. Figure 1's six average-shift labels and Figures 5/10a labels were inspected from the PDF in memory without creating image files. All 32 Table 1 rows (160 numeric cells) match the PDF text. Figure 4b's markers were counted from its decoded PDF vector stream, giving 43 + 29 + 27 = 99 observations; this is explicitly derived from the plotted marks, not a printed N or a whole-study analyzed count. The corresponding Figure 6 percentages were checked for compatibility, without assigning its analyzed denominator. No exclusion count or effect size was calculated. The four study entries retain three substantive analyses and a preliminary pilot phase; pilot/main participant overlap is unknown, and no pilot or historical-corpus counts are added to S1. All 14 reconciled outcomes are retained. Stance, argument/POS profiles and within-essay semantic/lexical changes are not reclassified as creativity or across-person diversity. Self-reported creativity remains scored_on_output=false. Robustness variants remain within outcome families. Self-reported voice (outside the output-outcome inventory): Human User 4.53, LLM-Influenced 4.48, LLM 3.37; heavy use versus control t(69) = 5.799, p < 0.001 (p. 8, Figure 4a and Section 4.1; survey item p. 24, Appendix A.6). Recommendation scores (outside the output-outcome inventory because they rate reviewed research): 4.43 for LLM reviews and 4.13 for human reviews; Section 4.8 describes these as 10% higher, whereas the abstract says a full point higher. These remain attributed source statements, without a derived difference; no SD, SE, CI or score-analysis N is supplied (p. 1, abstract; p. 14, Section 4.8). Other survey responses and illustrative essays/transcripts are not additional output-scored outcomes. S2-O1 n_units = 86 counts D1-D2 pairs per revision condition; other S2 units refer to source essays or paired changes per condition, not a total over generated revisions. S2 retains ai_vs_human because researchers produced automated counterfactual revisions of archived human drafts, rather than reanalyzing randomized AI assistance to people (pp. 5-7). S3 counts denote reviews, not people; Table 1 printed p = 0.0000 is rounded, not exact zero. Figure 10 panel captions and plot labels identify analytic scores as ArgRewrite-v2 and argument types as the human study; Section 4.7 reverses the dataset names. Figure 6 exact p = 0.017 and the compatible prose bound p < 0.036 are both preserved. The integrated supplement is documented in source.supplement. The blank data URL reflects the absence of a separately stated download URL; the code URL is printed on pp. 1 and 8. All seven prior open questions and the added pilot-overlap question are classified in final.open_items. None prevents the three eligibility decisions; unresolved Ns and absent diversity precision limit extraction/pooling. There are no unresolved reconciliation differences; final n_corrected/n_rejected/n_open count challenge dispositions only.

old.reason: S1 explicitly randomizes individuals to embedded gpt-4o-mini access or no AI during essay writing (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 22, Appendix A.3-A.4). The one-essay-per-participant task and Figure 4b's directly counted 99 essay observations support at least 50 analyzed writers (p. 4; p. 8, Figure 4b and its caption; p. 22). The 99 observations comprise 43 Human-User, 29 LLM-Influenced and 27 LLM markers, counted in the PDF vector graphics with the legend excluded; this is a figure-specific observation count, not a printed participant N. The methods report 100 randomized people allocated 45/55 and 28 LLM-Influenced users (pp. 4-5). These counts conflict with the plotted group counts, so exact overall and arm analyzed Ns remain null; neither an exclusion count nor another outcome's N is inferred. The paper computes semantic representations of participants' completed essays and compares spread across writers, satisfying the output-scored diversity criterion (pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and Section 4.2). Thus all three core criteria are met for S1 across_people. Self-reported creativity is not the qualifying outcome. Use intensity was not randomized, and the diversity evidence is figure-only: no scalar full-assigned-AI-versus-control diversity effect or participant-appropriate uncertainty is supplied for pooling. S2 is automated AI-versus-human revision context, not a reanalysis of an experiment assigning AI to people (pp. 5-7); S3 is observational review-content analysis; S4 is a small preliminary protocol pilot without a scored creativity/diversity outcome. Pilot, archived-student and reviewer counts are not added to S1. No after_ai output is reported.

open_items[1].item: A scalar diversity effect and participant-appropriate uncertainty for the full randomized S1 AI-access-versus-control contrast, and scalar S2 between-writer diversity evidence, are absent (pp. 1, 8-9, 26-34). Participant-linked essays, assigned arms and analysis data would allow an auditable reanalysis; this affects pooling, not the existence of the qualifying computed outcome.
